ACTS: Learning Visuo-Tactile World Models from Human Physical Interaction

Yuxiang Ma ††thanks: Equal contribution.    Weihan Xu11footnotemark: 1    Pengfei Ye    Anna Mei Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology  University of Washington  Harvard University    Yuxin Ray Song    Tingle Li   Haonan Chen   Edward H. Adelson Affiliation: University of California, Berkeley  Stanford University
Abstract

Action-conditioned world models for contact-rich manipulation require data that captures how contact forms, slides, and releases under varying force. Such data are slow to collect through robot teleoperation, which often lacks force feedback and is constrained by gripper geometry. We ask whether these dynamics can instead be learned from human physical interaction and transferred to a robot. We present ACTS, a visuo-tactile world model trained only on human interaction data. Operators manipulate handheld GelSight sensors while we record third-person and wrist video, tactile images, 6-DoF sensor motion, and tactile-derived normal force, yielding React, a 4.9-hour bimanual dataset across three objects. We represent actions at the tactile sensor as motion augmented by force change, providing a shared action space for human collection and robot execution. ACTS jointly predicts future scene, wrist, and tactile observations. On held-out human data, ACTS improves scene-view prediction by 0.7–2.0 dB PSNR over the stronger of two visuo-tactile world models trained from scratch on React. Without fine-tuning, in the robot teleoperation rollouts we inspected, predicted tactile imprints still appear and disappear with recorded contact. Visual transfer is less robust: camera predictions exceed frame copying on PushT, are mixed on Rope, and fall below it on Motherboard, while wrist views can blur or hallucinate structure. These results suggest that contact dynamics transfer more reliably than visual appearance from human to robot. Project website and supplementary videos: https://acts-anon.github.io/.

1 Introduction

Robot world models predict how candidate actions change future observations, supporting planning and policy learning (Zhu et al., 2025; Hou et al., 2026). Contact-rich manipulation is difficult to model because small changes in contact location and force can determine whether an object sticks, slides, jams, or loses contact. Vision captures scene motion but often cannot resolve the local interactions that cause it. Learning such dynamics therefore requires data spanning contact formation, loading, sliding, and release under varied geometry and force. Collecting this interaction data is the bottleneck we address.

Existing visuo-tactile world models are trained on robot interaction trajectories (Higuera et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026b), in one case combined with data from a handheld gripper (Zheng et al., 2026). In parallel, robot-free interfaces such as UMI and TacUMI collect human demonstrations with handheld devices  (Chi et al., 2024; Cheng et al., 2026). Robot teleoperation is slow for dense contact exploration and typically provides limited force feedback (Tang et al., 2026), while handheld grippers remove the robot but retain a fixed contact geometry. In both cases, actions are tied to the collection device. We instead define motion and contact at the tactile sensor, where the same action representation can be used by a human or a robot.

Human operators directly manipulate handheld GelSight sensors while we record 6-DoF sensor poses together with synchronized visual and tactile observations. We represent each action by relative sensor motion augmented with a force-informed displacement (Chen et al., 2025) along the sensor normal, derived from tactile-estimated normal force (Fig. 1). This interface allows operators to vary contact location, orientation, and loading without a gripper constraining how the sensor meets the object. Because the action is defined at the sensor rather than the hand that carries it, human collection and robot execution share the same sensor-level action space.

We use these interactions to train ACTS, a visuo-tactile world model adapted from a pretrained video model. Given observation history and sensor actions, ACTS jointly predicts future scene, wrist, and tactile observations. Each action is provided both as force-informed motion in the local sensor frame and as sensor geometry projected into the scene view. We collect React, 4.9 hours of curated bimanual interaction with three objects, including multi-view video, two GelSight Mini streams  (Johnson & Adelson, 2009; Yuan et al., 2017), tracked sensor poses, and tactile-derived normal force.

We train one model per object using only human data and evaluate zero-shot on robot teleoperation with the same sensing devices. ACTS outperforms visuo-tactile world-model baselines on held-out human scene prediction, while robot rollouts show that predicted tactile contact transitions can transfer without robot-specific fine-tuning. Visual transfer is less robust, revealing a remaining gap between human and robot appearance distributions.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    A sensor-level action representation that provides a common interface for human data collection and robot execution.

  • •

    React, a 4.9-hour human visuo-tactile dataset with tracked sensor poses and tactile-derived normal force.11 1 We will release the React dataset, trained models, and code upon acceptance.

  • •

    ACTS, a visuo-tactile world model trained only on human interaction data and evaluated zero-shot on robot teleoperation.

2 Related Work

World models for robot manipulation. World models learn action-conditioned dynamics for planning, simulation, policy learning, and evaluation (Hou et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). Visual-foresight methods planned through predicted image trajectories (Finn & Levine, 2017; Dasari et al., 2020), and recent models build on pretrained visual representations and video generators (Zhou et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2026). These models learn from robot trajectories, with actions given as end-effector motion, joint commands, or gripper states (Dasari et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2026), tying the learned dynamics to the robot that collected the data.

Visuo-tactile world models. Tactile sensing resolves contact that vision leaves ambiguous (Shan et al., 2026), and several world models now predict tactile futures. VT-WM (Higuera et al., 2026) jointly predicts visual and tactile latents for planning, ViTacWorld (Huang et al., 2026b) trains on combined real and simulated data, and OmniVTA (Zheng et al., 2026) pairs short-horizon visuo-tactile prediction with a contact-aware policy. ContactWorld (Zhang et al., 2026) compares visual and tactile representations for predictive planning, FeelWorld (Ma et al., 2026) predicts contact state, a force-related tactile latent, and slip, and Dream-Tac (Lou et al., 2026) and VT-WAM (Tian et al., 2026) couple tactile prediction with action generation. These models learn from robot trajectories; OmniVTA adds demonstrations from a handheld gripper (Cheng et al., 2026), so its actions remain those of a gripper. ACTS learns from human interaction with bare sensors instead, with actions defined at the tactile sensor so that the same representation describes a robot moving that sensor.

Visuo-tactile datasets. Visuo-tactile datasets record or simulate objects (Gao et al., 2022), human touch in natural scenes (Yang et al., 2022), spatially aligned visual–tactile samples (Dou et al., 2024), in-hand manipulation (Suresh et al., 2024), and data pooled across sensors (Zhao et al., 2025). They broaden tactile coverage but generally do not provide the action supervision a world model needs. Handheld collection systems do record actions: UMI (Chi et al., 2024) introduced robot-free demonstration collection, FreeTacMan, exUMI, and TacUMI add tactile, force, and richer motion sensing (Wu et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2026), and MimicTouch (Yu et al., 2025) records tactile demonstrations from the human hand. These systems target policy learning. React instead pairs visual and tactile observations with sensor-level motion and normal force, the supervision needed to train an action-conditioned world model.

3 Dataset

Human interaction data. React is collected by five operators performing bimanual interactions with a motherboard, a T-shaped block (PushT), and a rope. Each operator holds two independently movable devices, each equipped with a GelSight Mini vision-based tactile sensor (Yuan et al., 2017), an OptiTrack marker assembly for 6-DoF pose tracking, and a local camera. Three fixed cameras record the workspace (Fig. 4, Appendix A). Operators slide, pivot, push, and pull the objects while varying contact location, orientation, and loading. The data cover making and breaking contact, sticking, sliding, and object motion. Operators explore these contact conditions without pursuing a prescribed task goal. After curation, the human dataset contains 4.91 hours of interaction across 187 segments from 60 source recordings.

Robot evaluation data. We collect a separate bimanual evaluation set with two YAM arms controlled through GELLO teleoperation interfaces (Wu et al., 2024). Each arm carries the same handheld device used for human collection, with its GelSight Mini, marker assembly, and wrist camera, so robot and human episodes share sensors and action construction. Teleoperators perform non-prehensile manipulation with the same three objects. We record five one-minute episodes per object, yielding 15 episodes and 15 minutes of robot interaction. The world model is trained only on human interaction data; all robot episodes are held out for evaluation.

Post-processing. We align the visual, tactile, and pose streams by timestamp to a common 30 Hz timeline and retain flags that distinguish new tactile captures from repeated frames. We remove intervals with sensor freezes or tracking failures and divide the remaining data into contiguous valid segments. Normal-force estimates derived from the tactile images are combined with the tracked sensor motion to construct force-informed actions. Appendix A gives the alignment procedure, force-estimation method, and dataset statistics.

4 Method

We propose ACTS (Fig. 2), an action-conditioned world model jointly predicting future scene video, wrist views, and tactile observations from observation histories and actions for bimanual manipulation. We describe observation encoding and tokenization (Sec. 4.1), then force-aware sensor actions and view-aligned actions encoding contact-related motion and scene-view sensor geometry (Sec. 4.2). We detail unified sequence construction with spatiotemporal alignment and full-window action conditioning (Sec. 4.3), alongside the training objective and inference protocol (Sec. 4.4).

4.1 Multimodal Observation Representation

To capture manipulation from complementary perspectives, we jointly model scene video, wrist views, and tactile observations in a shared latent prediction framework. We define the observation streams as ℳ={V,WL,WR,TL,TR}\mathcal{M}=\{V,W^{L},W^{R},T^{L},T^{R}\}, where VV denotes the top-down scene RGB view, WLW^{L} and WRW^{R} denote the left and right wrist-camera RGB views, and TLT^{L} and TRT^{R} denote the corresponding GelSight observations. For each stream m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M}, let XHmX_{H}^{m} and XFmX_{F}^{m} denote its observed history and future sequence, respectively. Given synchronized histories and action conditions 𝒜\mathcal{A}, our goal is to model

pθ​({XFm}m∈ℳ∣{XHm}m∈ℳ,𝒜),p_{\theta}\!\left(\{X_{F}^{m}\}_{m\in\mathcal{M}}\mid\{X_{H}^{m}\}_{m\in\mathcal{M}},\mathcal{A}\right), (1)

where θ\theta denotes the model’s trainable parameters.

To obtain compact representations while preserving temporal causality, we encode each observation stream as

Zm=ℰm​(Xm),m∈ℳ,Z^{m}=\mathcal{E}_{m}(X^{m}),\qquad m\in\mathcal{M}, (2)

where XmX^{m} concatenates history XHmX_{H}^{m} and future XFmX_{F}^{m} in temporal order. The scene and two wrist-camera streams share the pretrained Wan2.2 causal VAE encoder (Wan et al., 2025), while both GelSight streams share a variant adapted to our visuo-tactile dataset.22 2 Details of tactile VAE adaptation are provided in Appendix D. All encoders are frozen, and observations are encoded offline. We partition ZmZ^{m} into history latents ZHmZ_{H}^{m} and future latent blocks ZFm=(z1m,…,zQm)Z_{F}^{m}=(z_{1}^{m},\ldots,z_{Q}^{m}). We spatially patchify each latent block and linearly project the patches into a common dd-dimensional token space, adding learned stream embeddings to distinguish their sources. Let 𝐞q,pm∈ℝd\mathbf{e}_{q,p}^{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the token for patch pp of future block qq in stream mm; history blocks are tokenized identically. The scene and two wrist-camera streams share one input projection and one output projection, while the two GelSight streams share a separate pair. The output projections map hidden states back to the corresponding latent patch spaces.

4.2 Action Representation

We connect motion, contact dynamics, and scene geometry through two complementary action representations. Following the trajectory-conditioned setting of IRASim (Zhu et al., 2025) and Cosmos3 (NVIDIA, 2026), we provide both representations for both hands over the complete window, collectively denoted by 𝒜\mathcal{A}, as clean conditions to every predicted observation block.

Force-aware sensor actions. Inspired by DexForce (Chen et al., 2025), we augment sensor-frame translation with a force-dependent normal displacement to capture contact-loading changes beyond observed motion. For hand hh at frame tt, let (Rth,𝐩th)(R_{t}^{h},\mathbf{p}_{t}^{h}) denote the sensor pose and fthf_{t}^{h} its estimated normal force. We define

Δ​Rth\displaystyle\Delta R_{t}^{h} =(Rth)⊤​Rt+1h,\displaystyle=(R_{t}^{h})^{\top}R_{t+1}^{h}, (3)
Δ​𝐩~th\displaystyle\Delta\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{t}^{h} =(Rth)⊤​(𝐩t+1h−𝐩th)+kf​Δ​fth​𝐧s,\displaystyle=(R_{t}^{h})^{\top}(\mathbf{p}_{t+1}^{h}-\mathbf{p}_{t}^{h})+k_{f}\Delta f_{t}^{h}\mathbf{n}_{s},
𝐚t+1h\displaystyle\mathbf{a}_{t+1}^{h} =[Δ​𝐩~th;Rot6D⁡(Δ​Rth)]∈ℝ9,\displaystyle=[\Delta\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{t}^{h};\operatorname{Rot6D}(\Delta R_{t}^{h})]\in\mathbb{R}^{9},

where Δ​fth=ft+1h−fth\Delta f_{t}^{h}=f_{t+1}^{h}-f_{t}^{h}, 𝐧s\mathbf{n}_{s} is the unit gel normal in sensor coordinates, kf=0.5​mm/Nk_{f}=0.5\,\mathrm{mm}/\mathrm{N}, and Rot6D\operatorname{Rot6D} is the 6-D rotation encoding of Zhou et al. (2019).

View-aligned actions. Inspired by Action Images (Zhen et al., 2026), we encode sensor position and orientation in the scene view using three sensor-fixed points: the gel center and offsets along the gel normal and an in-plane axis. For each sensor hh and frame tt, camera calibration maps these points to normalized pixel coordinates and camera-space depths, which we concatenate into 𝐮th∈ℝ9\mathbf{u}_{t}^{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{9}. Depth retains geometric information lost during projection. Appendix E details the force augmentation and reference-point projection.

4.3 Multimodal Sequence Construction

Sequence construction. To jointly predict future observations from history and actions, we pack clean history tokens, action tokens, and noisy future target tokens from all streams into a single sequence. We initialize the generator from pretrained Cosmos3 (NVIDIA, 2026) weights to adapt its spatiotemporal representations to visuo-tactile prediction. To preserve conditioning information, we corrupt only future target latents and apply noise-level embeddings only to their tokens.

Temporal alignment. To align observations and actions by physical time, we adopt Cosmos3’s multimodal rotary position embedding (MRoPE) (NVIDIA, 2026), which encodes time, height, and width in separate rotary dimensions. Each token is assigned a timestamp τi\tau_{i}, where observation tokens use latent-block endpoints, sensor-action tokens use transition endpoints, and view-aligned action tokens use their corresponding frames. We map these timestamps to a shared temporal axis using Cosmos3’s pretrained time scale, aligning streams in time while preserving spatial structure within observations.

Attention mask. To predict observation dynamics under a known action trajectory, we allow all tokens to access the complete action window while restricting attention to observation keys at the same or earlier timestamps. We implement this through an additive attention mask:

Mi​j={0,j∈ℐA​or​τj≤τi,−∞,otherwise,M_{ij}=\begin{cases}0,&j\in\mathcal{I}_{A}\ \text{or}\ \tau_{j}\leq\tau_{i},\\ -\infty,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (4)

where i,ji,j index query and key tokens within a sample, τi\tau_{i} denotes token time, and ℐA\mathcal{I}_{A} contains sensor-action and view-action token indices. Applied in every layer, this mask preserves temporal ordering in direct observation attention while allowing same-time tokens to exchange information across streams for joint prediction. To prevent ground-truth leakage, we additionally construct each prediction prefix without later observation blocks or clean copies of the current target in Sec. 4.4.

4.4 Training and Inference

Training. To learn sequential dynamics across observation streams, we train ACTS with blockwise teacher forcing. Each future block qq is predicted from clean observation history, preceding ground-truth future blocks, and the full action window, collectively denoted by 𝒞q\mathcal{C}_{q}. Following Cosmos3 (NVIDIA, 2026), we use rectified flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023) with noisy targets

z~qm=(1−σ)​zqm+σ​ϵqm,ϵqm∼𝒩⁡(0,I),\widetilde{z}_{q}^{m}=(1-\sigma)z_{q}^{m}+\sigma\epsilon_{q}^{m},\qquad\epsilon_{q}^{m}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), (5)

where mm indexes observation streams and σ\sigma is the noise level. The model jointly predicts velocities vqm,∗=ϵqm−zqmv_{q}^{m,*}=\epsilon_{q}^{m}-z_{q}^{m} by minimizing

ℒ=𝔼⁡[1Q​∑q=1Q∑m∈ℳ‖vθm​(Z~q,𝒞q,σ)−vqm,∗‖22Dz],\mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{Q}\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}}\frac{\left\|v_{\theta}^{m}(\widetilde{Z}_{q},\mathcal{C}_{q},\sigma)-v_{q}^{m,*}\right\|_{2}^{2}}{D_{z}}\right], (6)

where Z~q\widetilde{Z}_{q} collects the noisy target streams, QQ is the number of future blocks, and DzD_{z} is the number of scalar elements per stream’s latent block. Only current target tokens are corrupted and supervised.

Inference. To follow the sequential prediction process used during training, we generate future latent blocks autoregressively within each prediction window. Each block is conditioned on the observed history, previously generated blocks, and the complete action sequence. For the first block, the observation context contains only the recorded history. We initialize the target latents of all streams with independent Gaussian noise and jointly transform them into clean predictions by integrating the learned velocity field, while keeping the conditioning tokens fixed. The completed block is then appended as clean latent context for predicting the next block, replacing the ground-truth context used during teacher forcing. This process proceeds entirely in latent space without intermediate decoding. After all future blocks are generated, the corresponding decoders {𝒟m}m∈ℳ\{\mathcal{D}_{m}\}_{m\in\mathcal{M}} reconstruct the predicted latents into synchronized scene, wrist, and tactile observations. Appendix F provides further training and inference details.

5 Experiments

5.1 Baseline Models

We compare ACTS with two action-conditioned visuo-tactile world models, training both from scratch on React. Among recent visuo-tactile world models, only ContactWorld (Zhang et al., 2026) and Dream-Tac (Lou et al., 2026) release training code; VT-WM (Higuera et al., 2026), OmniVTA (Zheng et al., 2026), ViTacWorld (Huang et al., 2026b), FeelWorld (Ma et al., 2026), and VT-WAM (Tian et al., 2026) had not released model code at the time of writing. ContactWorld is a decoder-free JEPA-style (Assran et al., 2023) model, which we train with its official code, adapted to our observation and action spaces. VT-WM-style is our reimplementation of VT-WM, preserving its autoregressive latent predictor and action conditioning while adapting its interfaces to our data. We intended to compare with Dream-Tac but could not adapt it to React: it generates actions jointly with future observations instead of conditioning on given actions, and its released code expects a robot camera layout and proprioception that React lacks. Implementation details and deviations appear in Appendices I and G.

5.2 Evaluation Metrics

We compare ACTS with baseline models on future-frame prediction using held-out human recordings and zero-shot transfer to robot episodes.

Video Generation Metrics. Given eight observed frames (one for ContactWorld, its native context) and recorded actions, each model predicts the next eight frames (0.53 s at 15 fps). We evaluate only predicted frames, separately for the scene view, two wrist cameras, and two GelSight streams. We report PSNR for pixel-level fidelity, SSIM (Wang et al., 2004) for structural similarity, and LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018) for perceptual distance. Higher PSNR and SSIM and lower LPIPS indicate better results. For both human and robot data, reference frames are decoded from ground-truth latents using the frozen RGB and tactile VAEs. All comparisons use identical test windows and seeds. Appendix B provides further details.

Robot Experiments. We apply models trained on human data to held-out robot episodes (Sec. 3) without fine-tuning. Robot recordings are normalized to match the human data’s tactile color and illumination and wrist-camera tone. Actions are constructed from OptiTrack sensor poses and GelSight-estimated force following Sec. 4.2, as for the human data, rather than from robot joint readings. Per-step translations from forward kinematics differ from the OptiTrack ones by a median of 0.33 mm, about half the median per-step motion, so OptiTrack keeps robot actions consistent with the human training data (Appendix B). We use the same eight-frame observation and prediction protocol on windows in which contact is made or broken, and report the same per-stream metrics.

6 Results

6.1 Implementation Details

We train ACTS separately per task with the same architecture and training recipe, initializing from Cosmos3-Nano (NVIDIA, 2026). Observation VAEs and backbone weights remain frozen, while 45.3M parameters are trained through LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) and modality-specific interfaces. All ACTS models are trained for 20 epochs on four NVIDIA H100 GPUs, with training, validation, and test splits separated by source episode. Appendix F provides implementation and dataset details.

6.2 Qualitative Examples

Fig. 3 shows a held-out PushT window in which the operator lifts the left sensor off the block; more rollouts are on the project page. The recorded left imprint fades over t+1t{+}1–t+3t{+}3, and the predicted imprint fades on the same frames. The block stays in place, and the scene and wrist predictions remain consistent with the recording. Predicted imprints are slightly smoother than recorded ones, which we attribute to the tactile VAE.

6.3 Quantitative Results

Tab. 1 compares ACTS with a persistence baseline that repeats the last observed frame. ACTS improves all camera streams by 1.01.0–4.64.6 dB PSNR, indicating that it captures scene motion and wrist-camera ego-motion beyond temporal persistence. On the scene view, ACTS also outperforms ContactWorld and VT-WM-style on all three objects in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS (Tab. 2).

Tactile scores require more careful interpretation. GelSight observations change only locally during contact, so a copied frame already achieves high PSNR and SSIM over the short prediction horizon. ACTS shows little consistent gain in full-frame tactile PSNR, although LPIPS improves on all tactile streams. These metrics capture appearance, not whether contact is made or broken at the right time (Sec. 7), so we also inspect rollouts. Appendix H ablates the force term in the sensor action (Eq. 3): it changes camera-stream PSNR by at most 0.3 dB, never significantly, and tactile PSNR by at most 0.6 dB, yet in the window of Fig. 1b it decides whether an imprint forms when the sensor reaches the block.

6.4 Zero-Shot Transfer to Robot Teleoperation

Tab. 3 applies the same models, without fine-tuning, to held-out robot teleoperation, scored as in Tab. 1 against VAE-reconstructed ground truth. Robot motion is slower than human manipulation, so repeating the last frame is a stronger baseline than on human data. Transfer varies by object. On PushT, ACTS improves all three camera streams in PSNR and SSIM, by up to 2.12.1 dB PSNR on the scene view. On Rope, the results are mixed: scene PSNR rises by 0.70.7 dB while right-wrist PSNR drops by 0.40.4 dB. On Motherboard, ACTS falls below frame copying on every camera stream. Likely causes are its geometry, whose connectors, slots, and heat sinks put many fine edges in view, and the robot wrist cameras, which record it darker than the human data. Across objects, the wrist views degrade most: predictions are blurrier than on human data and sometimes contain object structure absent from the recording. On the tactile streams, frame copying scores higher PSNR on five of the six streams, by up to 2.12.1 dB, while ACTS scores lower LPIPS on five of the six.

Fig. 5 (Appendix C) shows a held-out robot PushT window in which the sensor breaks contact with the block. The predicted left GelSight imprint fades within one frame of the recorded one, and the scene prediction keeps the block in place. The left wrist view shows the failure described above: the recorded view barely changes, while the predicted block face grows and shifts from t+4t{+}4 onward. Across the robot rollouts we inspected, including those on the project page, predicted imprints appear and disappear as contact is made and broken in the recording, even where the wrist predictions degrade.

7 Limitations

Force estimation. The estimator predicts only normal force, which governs making and breaking contact but not the shear that governs sliding. Its error of 0.318 N (6.4%) is measured on CNC calibration data (Appendix A.3); the human recordings have no force ground truth, so its error during manipulation is unmeasured.

Evaluation metrics. All streams are scored against VAE-reconstructed ground truth, so errors shared by the model and the VAE go undetected. On GelSight images, full-frame metrics are dominated by static gel and do not show whether contact is made or broken at the right time, which we assess only qualitatively.

Motion capture. Sensor poses come from OptiTrack for both human collection and robot evaluation, which confines React to one instrumented lab. Forward kinematics is not a substitute: its per-step translations differ from OptiTrack by a median of 0.33 mm, about half the median per-step motion and equal to the force term for a 0.66 N change (Appendix B). Robot data collection and deployment therefore also need external tracking.

8 Conclusion

We presented ACTS, a visuo-tactile world model trained entirely on human physical interaction, with actions defined at the tactile sensor as motion augmented with force change. It predicts the scene view better than two visuo-tactile baselines on held-out human data, and on zero-shot robot teleoperation its tactile imprints track contact transitions while wrist views degrade. Improving visual transfer and using ACTS for robot planning are future work.

Ethics statement

React records five human operators who are members of the research team and gave informed consent to the recording and release of the data. The third-person cameras capture the operators’ hands and forearms, and no frame captures an operator’s face. The dataset contains no personal information beyond these recordings. The objects are inanimate, and the robot experiments involve no human subjects. We see no application of this work that raises concerns beyond those common to robot manipulation research.

Reproducibility statement

Appendix A describes data collection, stream alignment, curation, and normal-force estimation, with dataset statistics in Tab. 4. Appendix F gives the model architecture, training hyperparameters, data splits, and compute, and Appendix D the tactile VAE adaptation. Baseline configurations and every deviation from the published models are listed in Appendices I and G. Evaluation protocol and metrics are defined in Sec. 5.2, and all comparisons use identical test windows and seeds. We will release the React dataset, the trained models, and the training and evaluation code upon acceptance.

Use of generative AI

In this work, we used generative AI tools (Claude, Anthropic) to provide feedback on experimental design, to help interpret results, and to help build the automatic pipeline that cleans and reformats raw recordings into the dataset. We did not use generative AI tools to generate synthetic data, develop theoretical models or conceptual frameworks, propose or refine hypotheses, implement methods, or translate; formulating or proving mathematical claims and qualitative or thematic data analysis are not applicable to this work. Additionally, we used generative AI tools to create or edit software code, draft and edit parts of the paper, and identify and format references. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work. Experimental changes suggested by the AI tool, such as additional baselines and contact-timing metrics, were treated as proposals, and the authors decided which to pursue. The curation pipeline applies fixed rules, removing intervals with camera freezes or invalid pose tracking, and keeps the source-frame index of every aligned sample so that its output can be audited against the raw recordings (Appendix A). Every description of a qualitative result was checked against the corresponding figure by the authors, and every explanation of a quantitative result reflects the authors’ own analysis. Bibliography entries added with AI assistance were retrieved from their DOIs and checked against CrossRef, and no reference was written from the model’s memory. Appendix A Dataset and Force-Estimation Details

A.1 Dataset Composition

The curated dataset contains 529,839 aligned time steps from 60 source recordings. Removing intervals with invalid sensor or tracking data leaves 187 variable-length segments, totaling 4.91 hours at the nominal 30 Hz alignment rate. Multiple segments may come from the same source recording and therefore do not represent independent collection sessions. Table 4 gives the distribution across objects.

A.2 Temporal Alignment and Curation

Visual streams are recorded at a nominal 30 Hz and OptiTrack poses at 100 Hz. We align all modalities by timestamp to a common 30 Hz timeline. Because the tactile cameras operate at a lower frame rate, adjacent time steps may reuse the same tactile image. For each sensor, a freshness flag and source-frame index distinguish new captures from repeated observations.

We remove intervals containing camera freezes or invalid pose tracking and divide each recording into contiguous valid segments. Force is estimated for each new tactile capture and held constant on aligned rows that reuse the same image. We retain the source-frame indices to audit this alignment.

A.3 Normal-Force Estimation

We calibrate a sensor-specific normal-force estimator for the GelSight Mini (Yuan et al., 2017) sensors used in our collection setup. For each recording, we construct a reference image from low-contact observations and compute features describing the contact area, surface deformation, and RGB change relative to this reference.

We standardize these features and map them to normal force using support vector regression with a radial basis function kernel (RBF-SVR). The kernel provides a nonlinear mapping in which tactile observations with similar feature vectors receive similar force predictions. We train the regressor on separate CNC calibration data collected with known normal loads over 0.07–15.00 N. A reference-dependent noise gate suppresses responses near the no-contact state.

Position-grouped cross-validation on 4,709 CNC calibration samples gives a mean absolute error of 0.318 N (95% CI: 0.300–0.338 N) and a mean absolute percentage error of 6.40%. The percentage error is computed per sample relative to its measured force.

This calibration is specific to our sensors. Optical tactile images vary with the sensor unit, gel, illumination, camera response, and gel condition, so we do not assume that the mapping transfers unchanged to another sensor. The human interaction recordings also lack synchronized force ground truth. We use the estimates as approximate loading signals for action construction, not as measured force annotations.

Appendix B Evaluation Details

Prediction Protocol. Each test window contains eight observed frames followed by eight target frames, corresponding to a prediction horizon of approximately 0.53 s at 15 fps. Models receive the observed frames and recorded action sequence. We score only the predicted frames, separately for the scene camera, left and right wrist cameras, and left and right GelSight sensors (Yuan et al., 2017). All checkpoints and ablations are evaluated on identical test windows with identical random seeds.

Reference Frames. For both human recordings and robot episodes, reference frames are obtained by decoding ground-truth latents with the frozen RGB and tactile VAEs. These scores therefore measure prediction fidelity relative to VAE reconstructions rather than raw recordings.

Visuo-Tactile Prediction Metrics. We compute PSNR, SSIM (Wang et al., 2004), and LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018) independently for each stream. For a predicted window 𝐘^\widehat{\mathbf{Y}} and its reference 𝐘\mathbf{Y}, PSNR is

PSNR=10​log10​R2MSE⁡(𝐘^,𝐘),\operatorname{PSNR}=10\log_{10}\frac{R^{2}}{\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat{\mathbf{Y}},\mathbf{Y})}, (7)

where RR is the peak value of the image intensity range and the mean squared error is computed over all pixels, channels, and predicted frames in the window. PSNR measures pixel-level fidelity and is sensitive to spatial alignment and contact imprints, making it our primary metric for the low-texture tactile streams.

SSIM (Wang et al., 2004) compares local luminance, contrast, and structure. We compute it per predicted frame and average over the window. LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018) measures perceptual distance using pretrained AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al., 2012) features and is likewise averaged over predicted frames. Higher PSNR and SSIM and lower LPIPS indicate better fidelity.

Zero-Shot Robot Evaluation. Models trained on human recordings are applied to held-out robot episodes (Sec. 3) without fine-tuning. Before inference, robot observations are mapped to the human recording conventions for tactile color and illumination and wrist-camera tone. Action representations are constructed from OptiTrack sensor poses and GelSight-estimated force using the procedure in Sec. 4.2. We use OptiTrack rather than the robot’s joint readings so that human and robot actions are computed by the same pipeline from the same tracking system. The two sources disagree at the scale of a single step. Per-step translations computed from forward kinematics differ from those computed from OptiTrack by a median of 0.33 mm (90th percentile 0.99 mm), while the sensor moves a median of 0.60 mm per step (90th percentile 3.06 mm). Grouped by speed, the difference is 20–40% of the per-step motion, and it exceeds the motion when the robot is nearly still. Per-step rotations differ by a median of 0.1–0.2∘. Likely sources are the calibration between the robot base and the OptiTrack frame, joint backlash, and arm compliance under contact load, none of which forward kinematics observes. Actions built from forward kinematics would therefore depart from the human training data by a large fraction of each step, whereas OptiTrack measures the sensor directly in both settings. We select evaluation windows in which contact is made or broken and apply the same eight-frame observation and eight-frame prediction protocol. All metrics are computed per stream against the VAE-reconstructed reference frames described above.

Appendix C Qualitative Robot Rollouts

Fig. 5 shows a zero-shot rollout on a held-out robot episode from the evaluation set of Sec. 3, produced by the model trained only on human data and discussed in Sec. 6.4. Rollouts on all three objects are on the project page.

Appendix D Tactile Encoder

We adapt the pretrained causal 3D VAE of Wan2.2-TI2V-5B (Wan et al., 2025) to tactile video with LoRA, keeping all base weights frozen. Training uses 6,533 left and right gel-sensor videos (64 held out for validation) from visuo-tactile datasets including GelSLAM (Huang et al., 2026a), FeelAnyForce (Shahidzadeh et al., 2025), Tactile MNIST (Schneider et al., 2025), FoTa (Zhao et al., 2025), TacQuad (Feng et al., 2025), 3D Cal (Kota et al., 2026), and TactileTracking (Huang et al., 2025), covering 26 tasks that include manipulation, indentation, and object tracking. Each sample is a 17-frame clip resampled from 30 to 6 fps and center-cropped to 256×\times256. Rank-32 LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) adapters (α=32\alpha=32) go on all 72 convolutional layers of the encoder and decoder, 30.6M trainable parameters (4.2% of the VAE). The objective is an L1 reconstruction loss weighted by optical-flow magnitude, so regions of the gel that deform get more weight. The flow is AllTracker (Harley et al., 2025) reference flow from frame 0 to frame tt. Two more terms are added: a spatial-gradient (edge) L1 loss (weight 1.0) and LPIPS (weight 0.1). We train for 4,000 optimizer steps with AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019), learning rate 10−410^{-4} with 100 warmup steps, an effective batch size of 4 and bf16, on a single H100. Validation PSNR is 40.2 dB.

Appendix E Action Representation Details

Sensor-frame motion and force. For each hand h∈{L,R}h\in\{L,R\}, the sensor pose comprises an orientation Rth∈SO⁡(3)R_{t}^{h}\in\mathrm{SO}(3) and position 𝐩th∈ℝ3\mathbf{p}_{t}^{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} in a common reference frame. The estimated normal force fthf_{t}^{h} is obtained using the procedure in Appendix A.3.

Sensor pose captures motion but does not fully describe contact loading. Following the force-informed formulation of Chen et al. (2025), we interpret normal force as a virtual displacement along the sensor’s local pressing direction:

𝐩~th=𝐩th+kf​fth​Rth​𝐧s,\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{t}^{h}=\mathbf{p}_{t}^{h}+k_{f}f_{t}^{h}R_{t}^{h}\mathbf{n}_{s}, (8)

where 𝐧s\mathbf{n}_{s} is the unit gel normal in sensor coordinates and kf=0.5​mm/Nk_{f}=0.5\,\mathrm{mm}/\mathrm{N} is an assumed controller compliance. The orientation remains unchanged. As illustrated in Fig. 1a, the offset represents a virtual controller displacement, not a measurement of gel compression.

To construct actions, we express relative motion in the sensor coordinate system at frame tt and augment its translation with the change in force-induced displacement:

Δ​Rth\displaystyle\Delta R_{t}^{h} =(Rth)⊤​Rt+1h,\displaystyle=(R_{t}^{h})^{\top}R_{t+1}^{h}, (9)
Δ​𝐩th\displaystyle\Delta\mathbf{p}_{t}^{h} =(Rth)⊤​(𝐩t+1h−𝐩th),\displaystyle=(R_{t}^{h})^{\top}(\mathbf{p}_{t+1}^{h}-\mathbf{p}_{t}^{h}),
Δ​𝐩~th\displaystyle\Delta\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{t}^{h} =Δ​𝐩th+kf​Δ​fth​𝐧s,\displaystyle=\Delta\mathbf{p}_{t}^{h}+k_{f}\Delta f_{t}^{h}\mathbf{n}_{s},

where Δ​fth=ft+1h−fth\Delta f_{t}^{h}=f_{t+1}^{h}-f_{t}^{h}. The force increment is applied directly along the local normal, rather than obtained by differencing the virtual positions in Eq. 8. Concatenating the augmented translation with the six-dimensional rotation representation of Zhou et al. (2019) gives

𝐚t+1h=[Δ​𝐩~th;Rot6D⁡(Δ​Rth)]∈ℝ9.\mathbf{a}_{t+1}^{h}=[\Delta\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{t}^{h};\operatorname{Rot6D}(\Delta R_{t}^{h})]\in\mathbb{R}^{9}. (10)

The index t+1t+1 identifies the transition endpoint.

Reference-point projection. We define three fixed points in sensor coordinates:

𝐨1=𝐨c,𝐨2=𝐨c+ℓn​𝐧s,𝐨3=𝐨c+ℓp​𝐞s,\mathbf{o}_{1}=\mathbf{o}_{c},\qquad\mathbf{o}_{2}=\mathbf{o}_{c}+\ell_{n}\mathbf{n}_{s},\qquad\mathbf{o}_{3}=\mathbf{o}_{c}+\ell_{p}\mathbf{e}_{s}, (11)

where 𝐨c\mathbf{o}_{c} is the gel center, 𝐞s\mathbf{e}_{s} is a unit in-plane axis, and ℓn\ell_{n} and ℓp\ell_{p} are fixed offset distances. These points jointly encode sensor position and orientation.

Their coordinates in the common reference frame are 𝐪t,jh=Rth​𝐨j+𝐩th\mathbf{q}_{t,j}^{h}=R_{t}^{h}\mathbf{o}_{j}+\mathbf{p}_{t}^{h}. Using the calibrated transformation (RC,𝐭C)(R_{C},\mathbf{t}_{C}) from this frame to the scene camera, we obtain

𝐪t,jC,h=RC​𝐪t,jh+𝐭C,zt,jh=[𝐪t,jC,h]3.\mathbf{q}_{t,j}^{C,h}=R_{C}\mathbf{q}_{t,j}^{h}+\mathbf{t}_{C},\qquad z_{t,j}^{h}=[\mathbf{q}_{t,j}^{C,h}]_{3}. (12)

We project each point using the scene-camera calibration and normalize its pixel coordinates to obtain (x¯t,jh,y¯t,jh)(\bar{x}_{t,j}^{h},\bar{y}_{t,j}^{h}). Concatenating these coordinates and camera-space depths for all three points produces 𝐮th∈ℝ9\mathbf{u}_{t}^{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{9}. Unlike 𝐚t+1h\mathbf{a}_{t+1}^{h}, which describes a transition, 𝐮th\mathbf{u}_{t}^{h} describes sensor geometry at frame tt.

Action construction and normalization. Sensor and view actions each have nine dimensions per hand. We use 𝐧s=(0,−1,0)⊤\mathbf{n}_{s}=(0,-1,0)^{\top} and kf=5×10−4​m/Nk_{f}=5\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m/N}. Rot6D concatenates the first two columns of the relative rotation matrix. View conditions contain (x/W,y/H,d)(x/W,y/H,d) for each of the three reference points, with depth dd in meters. Sensor and view representations are normalized separately, pooling both hands to estimate training-set percentiles:

b~j=2​bj−q0.01,jq0.99,j−q0.01,j−1.\widetilde{b}_{j}=2\frac{b_{j}-q_{0.01,j}}{q_{0.99,j}-q_{0.01,j}}-1. (13)

Appendix F Implementation and Training Details

F.1 Data Preparation

Dataset splits. We train separate models for PushT, Rope, and Motherboard using the same architecture and training recipe. Each dataset is partitioned by complete source episodes, preventing windows from the same episode from appearing in different splits. Table 5 reports episode counts, window counts, and optimization steps per epoch. The PushT training set excludes windows with invalid action transitions. For Motherboard, two test episodes are in-distribution, while three were recorded in a separate session with different hardware and force calibration and are treated as out-of-distribution. Wrist observations are available in every episode.

Observation preprocessing. We sample all five observation streams at 15 fps and resize and center-crop frames to 256×256256\times 256. Each window contains eight history frames and eight future frames. The scene and two wrist streams use the pretrained Wan2.2-TI2V-5B VAE (Wan et al., 2025), while both tactile streams use its GelSight-specific (Yuan et al., 2017) LoRA-adapted variant. All VAEs remain frozen, and observation latents are encoded offline and cached. The VAEs produce 48-channel latents with temporal and spatial compression factors of four and sixteen. We prepend a copy of the initial frame before encoding and remove the resulting anchor latent, obtaining 48×4×16×1648\times 4\times 16\times 16 latents per stream. The four latent blocks comprise two history blocks and two future blocks. Spatial patches of size 2×22\times 2 yield an 8×88\times 8 token grid per block, with 192 input features per token.

F.2 Model Initialization and Adaptation

Backbone. We initialize the generator branch of Cosmos3-Nano (NVIDIA, 2026) from the official checkpoint. It contains 36 transformer layers with hidden dimension 4,096. The understanding branch is not used. We retain the pretrained generator, RGB input and output projections, final normalization layers, and noise-level embedder. The native action projection is replaced by our action interfaces, initialized from its pretrained weights. Each task starts independently from the same checkpoint with fresh adapters and interfaces, without warm-starting from another task’s trained model.

LoRA adapters. The base generator remains frozen. We apply LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) with rank 1616 and scaling parameter α=32\alpha=32 to the query, key, value, output, gate, up, and down projections in every transformer layer. These 36×7=25236\times 7=252 linear layers introduce 43.6M trainable parameters. The LoRA matrices AA and BB are initialized with Kaiming-uniform values and zeros, respectively, yielding zero initial adapter updates.

Modality interfaces. The scene and wrist streams share the frozen RGB input and output projections. Both tactile streams share a trainable projection pair initialized from the corresponding RGB projections. Sensor and view actions use separate nine-dimensional input projections, each shared by both hands. These projections are initialized from the first nine input channels of the UMI-domain slice of the pretrained action-conditioning projection. All input projections map to the same hidden dimension.

Stream embeddings and parameter count. A learned 9×40969\times 4096 embedding distinguishes five observation streams and four action streams. The embeddings are initialized from a truncated normal distribution, with action-stream rows additionally offset by the pretrained action-modality embedding. Together, the LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) adapters, tactile and action projections, and stream embeddings contain 45.3M trainable parameters, approximately 0.30% of the 15.2B backbone. The RGB projections and noise-level embedder remain frozen.

F.3 Sequence Packing and Temporal Alignment

Token layout. We concatenate streams into contiguous slices, ordering observation tokens by latent block, patch row, and patch column. A complete window contains 5×4×64=1,2805\times 4\times 64=1{,}280 observation tokens, 2×15=302\times 15=30 sensor-action tokens, and 2×16=322\times 16=32 view-action tokens, totaling 1,342 tokens. Each token retains its stream identity, frame index, spatial coordinates, and target indicator. Positional coordinates and attention masks are derived from this metadata rather than storage offsets.

Temporal and spatial coordinates. All streams use a shared 15 fps clock. Observation blocks receive the endpoint indices 3,7,11,153,7,11,15 of their four-frame intervals. Sensor-action tokens receive transition endpoints 1,…,151,\ldots,15, and view-action tokens receive frame indices 0,…,150,\ldots,15. We convert frame index kk to the pretrained temporal scale:

τ⁡(k)=rC​kr,r=15,rC=6.\tau(k)=r_{\mathrm{C}}\frac{k}{r},\qquad r=15,\quad r_{\mathrm{C}}=6. (14)

Observation tokens use patch row and column indices as spatial coordinates. Both spatial coordinates are zero for action tokens. Frame indices retain their original values across prediction prefixes within a window, so extending the prefix does not change existing token coordinates.

F.4 Training Procedure

Teacher-forcing prefixes. For each future block qq, we construct a separate prediction prefix with clean context

𝒞q=(ZH,ZF,<q,𝒜),\mathcal{C}_{q}=\left(Z_{H},Z_{F,<q},\mathcal{A}\right), (15)

where ZH={ZHm}m∈ℳZ_{H}=\{Z_{H}^{m}\}_{m\in\mathcal{M}} contains observation histories, ZF,<q={(z1m,…,zq−1m)}m∈ℳZ_{F,<q}=\{(z_{1}^{m},\ldots,z_{q-1}^{m})\}_{m\in\mathcal{M}} contains preceding ground-truth future blocks, and 𝒜\mathcal{A} contains both action representations for both hands over the complete window. The current target appears only in noisy form. Later observation blocks and clean copies of the current target are excluded to prevent ground-truth leakage. We apply the attention mask in Sec. 4.3, retaining access to the full action trajectory.

Each window produces two teacher-forced passes. The first contains two history blocks and the first future block from each stream, while the second additionally includes the preceding future block as clean context. With all 62 action tokens retained, these prefixes contain 1,022 and 1,342 tokens, respectively. Each pass contains 320 current target tokens. Their losses contribute equally to one optimizer update.

Noise sampling. We sample one noise level σ\sigma per window and share it across both target blocks and all observation streams. Following the pretrained generator’s Waver rule with shift parameter 3.03.0, we sample

ξ\displaystyle\xi ∼𝒰⁡(0,1),\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1), (16)
η\displaystyle\eta =1−ξ−1.29​[cos2⁡(π​ξ2)−1+ξ],\displaystyle=1-\xi-1.29\left[\cos^{2}\!\left(\frac{\pi\xi}{2}\right)-1+\xi\right], (17)
σ\displaystyle\sigma =3​η1+2​η.\displaystyle=\frac{3\eta}{1+2\eta}. (18)

Gaussian noise ϵqm\epsilon_{q}^{m} is sampled independently for each block and stream, with identity covariance. History, preceding ground-truth blocks, and actions remain clean. Noise-level embeddings are applied only to current target observation tokens.

Flow-matching supervision. The interpolation in Eq. 5 defines the target velocity vqm,∗=ϵqm−zqmv_{q}^{m,*}=\epsilon_{q}^{m}-z_{q}^{m}. In Eq. 6, each stream’s squared error is normalized by its latent-block size DzD_{z}. Stream losses are summed with equal weight and averaged over future blocks. We apply no additional noise-dependent loss weighting, and clean context tokens receive no prediction loss. The expectation is over training windows and sampled noise.

Optimization. We use AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) with learning rate 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}, (β1,β2)=(0.9,0.95)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.95), and weight decay 0.010.01. The learning rate warms up for 100 steps and remains constant thereafter. Gradients are clipped to a global norm of 1.01.0. Training uses four NVIDIA H100 GPUs with two windows per GPU, giving a global batch size of eight. Trainable parameters are maintained in FP32 with BF16 autocast, and activation checkpointing is enabled. Each model is trained for 20 epochs, with a checkpoint saved after every epoch.

F.5 Inference and Rollout

Within-window generation. Inference follows the training prefix construction, replacing preceding ground-truth future blocks with generated latents. For each target block, all streams are initialized with independent Gaussian noise and jointly denoised using UniPC with 35 steps, without classifier-free guidance. The sampler integrates the learned velocity field from noise to clean latents, corresponding to σ=1\sigma=1 to σ=0\sigma=0. Only current target latents are updated. Observed history, previously generated blocks, and the complete action window remain fixed. The first generated block serves directly as clean latent context for the second, without intermediate decoding or re-encoding. After restoring the VAE anchor, the corresponding decoders {𝒟m}m∈ℳ\{\mathcal{D}_{m}\}_{m\in\mathcal{M}} reconstruct the eight predicted frames per stream.

Across-window rollout. To extend generation beyond one window, we use the eight predicted frames as the next observation history. For each stream, we prepend a copy of its first predicted frame and re-encode the sequence, obtaining a new anchor and two history latent blocks. We advance the action window by eight frames and reset the temporal origin for the next prediction window. Thus, blocks within a window share latent context directly, while successive windows pass context through decoded and re-encoded observations.

Appendix G VT-WM-style Baseline

Predictor. A 12-layer transformer, hidden dimension 384, 6 heads, MLP ratio 4; 116.6 M parameters. Inputs are the cached Wan2.2 latents our model uses: 48×4×16×1648\times 4\times 16\times 16 per stream, five streams, 2×22\times 2 patches giving 64 tokens per latent block. Attention is factorized into spatial and temporal passes with axial RoPE. The three camera streams share an input projection and output head; the two tactile streams share a second pair. Training minimizes L1L_{1} on the next latent block, teacher-forced and sampled losses weighted equally, with the horizon-4 rollout generated without gradients.

Action conditioning. After every self-attention block, camera and tactile tokens cross-attend to action tokens, which carry sinusoidal positional embeddings. Actions are the force-informed sensor deltas our model receives, 36 dimensions per frame. One latent transition spans five frames; each receives its five raw transitions concatenated (180 dimensions) rather than averaged, since averaging shares raw transitions 3, 7 and 11 between adjacent latent transitions and leaks a later action into an earlier prediction. Latent block tt is conditioned on the action producing block t+1t{+}1, the block it is supervised against.

Training. AdamW, peak learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, (β1,β2)=(0.9,0.95)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.95), weight decay 0.01, gradient clipping at 1.0, 500 warmup steps into cosine decay. Batch size 8 with accumulation 4, bfloat16, one A100-80GB, 10 epochs. Early stopping is off so every task gets the same budget.

Deviations. (i) The cross-attention residual is gated by a zero-initialized scalar; the backbone relies on adaLN-zero identity at initialization, which an ungated sub-layer breaks. (ii) Context is eight frames at 15 fps (0.53 s) rather than nine at 6 fps (1.5 s), inherited from our encoder. (iii) Tactile tokens come from our GelSight tokenizer rather than Sparsh-X (Higuera et al., 2025) on Digit 360 (Lambeta et al., 2024), which needs audio, IMU and pressure channels this dataset lacks. (iv) Three camera views rather than one, matching our model’s inputs. (v) 116.6 M parameters for 20 epochs on one GPU, against 173 M for 80k updates on 32 A100s.

Validation. Before training we check identity at initialization, action reachability, temporal causality and gate-gradient flow. During training we track action gain: rollout L1L_{1} under a held control action divided by the same under the recorded action. A value near 1 means the model ignores its conditioning, which validation loss cannot detect. The control is Rot6D⁡(I)\mathrm{Rot6D}(I) with zero translation, not a zero vector: an all-zero rotation is degenerate and never occurs in training. Our runs reach 1.47–1.87.

Checkpoint selection. ACTS and VT-WM-style are evaluated at their final epoch. VT-WM-style’s validation L1L_{1} bottoms at epoch 4–6, but we do not select on it: L1L_{1} is minimized by the conditional mean, and across the nine camera task–stream pairs the best-validation checkpoint wins on PSNR and loses on LPIPS in eight. Action gain also rises monotonically to the final epoch on all three tasks while rollout L1L_{1} bottoms mid-training. Selecting on validation instead moves scene-view PSNR by under 0.1 dB on all three tasks and 0.4–0.7 dB on the motherboard wrist streams, and changes no conclusion.

Appendix H Force-Informed Action Ablation

Tab. 6 compares models trained with and without the force term, on identical test windows. Both are trained for 10 epochs rather than the 20 used for Tab. 1, which halves the cost of the ablation. The 20-epoch models of Tab. 1 differ from the 10-epoch force-informed models by up to 0.6 dB PSNR per stream, so only the paired comparison within Tab. 6 is meaningful. Scene and wrist PSNR change by at most 0.3 dB and never significantly, as expected: the force term only alters the normal component of the sensor action. Tactile PSNR differs by at most 0.6 dB. The differences are significant for both PushT tactile streams (PSNR), the left Motherboard sensor (SSIM and LPIPS), and the right Rope sensor, where PSNR drops by 0.3 dB.

These averages hide what the term does. Contact changes occupy few windows and an imprint occupies few pixels, so frame metrics are dominated by static gel. Fig. 6 shows a PushT window in which the right sensor touches the block. The pose-only action advances the sensor 21.7 mm along the gel normal over the eight predicted steps, 20.1 mm of it before contact; the force term adds 1.2 mm in total, up to 0.66 mm per step. Yet only the force-conditioned model forms an imprint. The sensor-frame pose says that the sensor advances, not where the block surface is; the force change marks the contact. The pose-only prediction stays blank and still scores slightly higher PSNR, since a blank gel costs less than a faint, slightly displaced imprint. The converse case, a release in which the pose-only model holds the imprint two frames past lift-off (43.8 vs. 37.0 dB), is on the project page: there the pose moves under 1 mm along the normal while the force-informed action retreats 1.9 mm.

Appendix I ContactWorld Baseline

ContactWorld (Zhang et al., 2026) is an action-conditioned visuo-tactile world model based on JEPA, with modality-specific CNN encoders and a GRU latent predictor but no image decoder. Each model observes one visual and one tactile stream with single-frame context. After verifying our setup using its released simulation checkpoints, we train ContactWorld from scratch using the official code and hyperparameters for approximately 100k steps. We use the same training episodes, source frames, 36-dimensional normalized actions, and held-out evaluation windows as ACTS.

Five-stream evaluation. To cover all five observation streams without modifying the architecture, we train three models per task on (scene, tactile-left), (wrist-left, tactile-left), and (wrist-right, tactile-right). Scene predictions come from the first model, left wrist and tactile predictions from the second, and right wrist and tactile predictions from the third. Each model retains its original two-stream, single-frame context, whereas ACTS conditions on all five streams over eight frames.

Pixel-space readout. We freeze the trained ContactWorld models and fit a separate readout for each output stream to enable pixel-space evaluation. Each readout maps four consecutive predicted ContactWorld latents, each comprising 512-dimensional visual and tactile embeddings, to one temporally compressed Wan2.2 (Wan et al., 2025) latent block. A two-layer MLP embeds these latents and broadcasts its output over the spatial latent grid. Conditioned additionally on the last ground-truth history VAE latent, four convolutional layers predict a residual relative to that history latent. Each readout contains approximately 1.5M parameters and uses a zero-initialized output layer. Readouts are trained on the GRU’s own rollouts from training windows using latent-space MSE and validation early stopping, while ContactWorld remains frozen. Predicted VAE latents are decoded and evaluated using the same modality-specific VAEs and metrics as ACTS.

We additionally evaluate an oracle-input condition using encoded ground-truth future frames and a context-only control replacing ContactWorld latents with their training-set mean. These conditions assess readout performance without latent rollout error and without predictive latent information, respectively.
